questions.question: What is duck typing in Ruby?
questions.title: Duck Typing
questions.direct_answer: Duck typing: 'If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck.' In Ruby, you don't check an object's class — you call its methods. `def speak(x); x.sound; end` works for any object with a `sound` method (Dog, Cat, Car), regardless of class. You rely on behavior, not type. This makes code flexible: a method accepting `#each` works with Array, Hash, Range, Set, your custom Enumerable. Compare to static typing where you'd declare a parameter type. Duck typing favors calling the method and rescuing NoMethodError (or letting it surface) over `is_a?` checks. The risk: an object might have the method but do the wrong thing (a `sound` that returns a number). Tests and clear contracts mitigate this. Use `respond_to?` only when you must branch; otherwise just call the method.

sections.title: Duck typing
sections.content:
```ruby
# Duck typing: rely on BEHAVIOR (methods), not class
class Dog;  def sound; 'Woof';  end; end
class Cat;  def sound; 'Meow';  end; end
class Car;  def sound; 'Vroom'; end; end

def speak(x)
  x.sound        # works for ANY object with a `sound` method
end
speak(Dog.new)   # 'Woof'
speak(Cat.new)   # 'Meow'
speak(Car.new)   # 'Vroom'  (no class check needed)

# Same with iteration: anything with `each` works
def total(coll)
  sum = 0
  coll.each { |x| sum += x }   # Array, Hash, Range, Set, custom
  sum
end
total([1, 2, 3])           # 6
total(1..3)                # 6  (Range responds to each)

# DON'T over-check types:
# def speak(x)
#   return 'woof' if x.is_a?(Dog)
#   return 'meow' if x.is_a?(Cat)   # brittle, not extensible
# end

# Use respond_to? only when you MUST branch:
def safe_sound(x)
  if x.respond_to?(:sound)
    x.sound
  else
    '...'
  end
end

# Risk: a `sound` that returns a number still 'works' but may be wrong.
# Mitigate with tests + clear contracts. Prefer calling the method.
```
